title: Priming vs Decode: Stream-Oriented Playbook and Scheduling Heuristics
content:
TL;DR
This is a practical playbook for managing the boundary between 'priming' (what we historically called prefill) and decode stages in the serving runtime. It focuses on stream overlap, micro-batch sizing, token-priority lanes, and KV-cache residency strategies that reduce P99 tail without blowing up cost.

Goals and constraints
- Primary: Meet streaming latency SLOs (50–200ms target tiers) while maximizing GPU utilization.
- Secondary: Keep token unit cost predictable; avoid frequent KV eviction churn.
- Constraints: heterogeneous model families, variable user prompt lengths, enforced per-tenant isolation (Dedicated).

Key idea summary
1) Treat priming as a best-effort, precompute-heavy stage that can be paused/resumed based on decoding pressure.
2) Expose an explicit priority score per stream computed from deadline, progress, and cache affinity. Scheduler uses score to allocate decode slots and priming microbatches.
3) Implement a lightweight shadow-KV for speculative priming that reduces residency churn when priming is abandoned.

Priority score (proposed)
- score = w_deadline * deadline_score + w_progress * progress_score + w_affinity * affinity_score - w_cost * estimated_gpu_seconds
- deadline_score = max(0, (deadline - now) / deadline_window) clamped 0..1
- progress_score = fraction of tokens already satisfied (higher => lower priority)
- affinity_score = fraction of priming KV keys already resident on target device (0..1)
- weights tuned per tier; example: w_deadline=0.5, w_affinity=0.3, w_progress=0.2

Scheduling heuristics
- Lane types: interactive (low-latency, single token stream), streaming (multi-token near-realtime), batch (high throughput).
- Reserve decode slots: small pool (5–10%) reserved for high-priority interactive streams to prevent head-of-line blocking.
- Priming policy: speculative priming only if affinity_score >= 0.6 OR expected decode wait > priming_threshold_ms.
- Microbatch sizing: prefer microbatch sizes that align with kernel-execution sweet spots (empirical: 4,8,16 tokens for our int8 kernels). Use dynamic growth: start at 4, grow if queue depth > N and tail latency stable.

KV cache management
- Shadow-KV: short-lived KV store for priming writes. Shadow entries have TTL << resident KV and do not trigger full device residency until promoted.
- Promotion: when decode request arrives that matches a shadow prefix AND affinity_score >= promotion_threshold, promote the shadow entry to resident KV; else discard on TTL expiry.
- Eviction policy: LRU weighted by active-stream-hopcount and next-decode-probability. Penalize eviction of items with high affinity across multiple streams.
- KV sharding note: avoid shard-hopping during priming; prefer to pin a priming microbatch to the shard that maximizes overlap probability.

Kernel affinity and decode windowing
- Maintain kernel profiles per-model for small-seq vs long-seq decode kernels. Scheduler prefers to group microbatches to keep kernel warm.
- Elastic decode window: allow high-throughput streams to request 'decode windows' of N tokens to reduce kernel switch overhead, but cap windows for interactive lanes.

Backpressure & graceful degradation
- If decode slot pressure > threshold, throttle priming by increasing priming_threshold_ms (defer speculative priming).
- If KV resident memory is close to limit, preferentially evict shadow-KV first, then low-affinity resident entries.
- Fallback model routing: when capacity constrained, route to compact quantized variants with automatic temperature adjustment to preserve output quality.

Experimentation & microbenchmarks (summary of local runs)
- Setup: 8xA100 fractional tests, workload mix 60% interactive/30% streaming/10% batch.
- Baseline (no shadow-KV, speculative priming always): P95 340ms, P99 980ms, GPU utilization 42%.
- With priority-score + reserved decode slots + shadow-KV: P95 210ms, P99 420ms, GPU utilization 58%.
- Microbatch growth policy cut token-unit cost by ~18% on steady streaming workloads.

Operator playbook (how to test/configure flags)
- flags: priming_enabled (bool), priming_threshold_ms (int), shadow_kv_ttl_ms (int), reserved_decode_percent (int), affinity_promotion_threshold (float)
- smoke test: 1) enable shadow-KV with TTL 2000ms; 2) set reserved_decode_percent=8; 3) run mixed workload for 15m and compare P95/P99.

Pseudocode (scheduler loop sketch)
- while true:
-   collect pending streams and compute score for each
-   allocate reserved interactive slots first
-   fill remaining decode capacity by descending score, grouping by kernel affinity
-   schedule priming microbatches based on leftover GPU cycles and priming_threshold_ms

Rollout plan
- Stage 0: internal canary on dev cluster (1 week) with telemetry hooks for score distribution and priming churn.
- Stage 1: opt-in beta for power users on Hosted API (2 weeks); collect regression on output quality and latency.
- Stage 2: gradual ramp to 25% traffic, monitor evictions and KV promotion rate.

Open questions (needs follow-up experiments)
- How well does shadow-KV interact with cross-tenant dedup caching? (risk: memory blowup)
- Optimal affinity heuristic across multi-GPU placements when KV sharding reshuffles.
- Tuning of weights (w_deadline, etc.) across different customer SLAs; automated RL tuning?

Notes to self / TODOs
- Add dashboard for "priming churn" (primed->promoted ratio, TTL expiries)
- Simulate extreme tail workloads (bursty short prompts) and measure reorder penalties
- Write unit tests for promotion path and eviction scoring

References and links
- linked_artifacts: confluence:INFR-priming-arch-2025, github:repo/serving-runtime/pull/842
- Related reading: kernel-warmup patterns, multi-tenant KV eviction literature

End of playbook (working draft)
This doc intentionally mixes heuristics, experiments, and operational steps. Feedback welcome; next iteration will include concrete config knobs and a small simulation harness for easier weight tuning.
